name: email-pkcs9-dn-embedded-nul-evades-constraint-invalid
description: permittedSubtrees rfc822Name is example.com (a domain-only constraint). The leaf has no SAN; instead its subject DN carries the legacy PKCS#9 emailAddress attribute (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.1, IA5String) with a value whose bytes are 'user@example.com', then 00, then 'evil.com'. RFC 5280 4.2.1.10 explicitly directs implementations to apply rfc822Name constraints to the subject field 'when the subject field contains an emailAddress attribute' — so this DN attribute is in scope of the constraint check. The full IA5String is not user@example.com and so the leaf must be rejected. A validator that hands the emailAddress to a C-string comparator will read 'user@example.com', accept it as inside the constraint, and let 'evil.com' through.
references: RFC 5280 4.2.1.6 (legacy emailAddress attribute deprecated but interpreted)
RFC 5280 4.2.1.10 (rfc822Name constraints apply to subject DN emailAddress)
notes: Constructed via subject_der_ascii2der so the NUL byte inside the IA5String is unambiguous in the source. cryptography's NameAttribute API rejects NUL in IA5 string attributes.

Without a SAN, RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10's directive to apply rfc822Name constraints to the subject emailAddress attribute is the only enforcement hook. GnuTLS in particular does this fallback explicitly (lib/x509/name_constraints.c gnutls_x509_name_constraints_check_crt RFC822NAME branch) — this case probes whether that fallback is C-string- or length-bounded.

certs.subject: C=US,O=NC Tests,CN=PKCS9 Email NUL Leaf
certs.subject_der_ascii2der: SEQUENCE { SET { SEQUENCE { OBJECT_IDENTIFIER { 2.5.4.6 } PrintableString { "US" } } } SET { SEQUENCE { OBJECT_IDENTIFIER { 2.5.4.10 } UTF8String { "NC Tests" } } } SET { SEQUENCE { OBJECT_IDENTIFIER { 2.5.4.3 } UTF8String { "PKCS9 Email NUL Leaf" } } } SET { SEQUENCE { OBJECT_IDENTIFIER { 1.2.840.113549.1.9.1 } IA5String { `75736572406578616d706c652e636f6d006576696c2e636f6d` } } } }
